text: 1362 IEEE JOURNAL OF SELECTED TOPICS IN SIGNAL PROCESSING, VOL. 19, NO. 7, OCTOBER 2025 A Review of Faithfulness Metrics for Hallucination Assessment in Large Language Models Ben Malin , Member, IEEE , Tatiana Kalganova , and Nikolaos Boulgouris , Senior Member, IEEE Abstract —This review examines the means with which faithful- ness has been evaluated across open-ended summarization, ques- tion answering and machine translation tasks. We ﬁnd that the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as a faithfulness evaluator is commonly the metric that is most highly correlated with human judgement. The means with which other studies have mitigated hallucinations is discussed, with both retrieval augmented gener- ation (RAG) and prompting framework approaches having been linked with superior faithfulness, whilst other recommendations for mitigation are provided. Research into faithfulness is integral to the continued widespread use of LLMs, as unfaithful responses can pose major risks to many areas whereby LLMs would other- wise be suitable. Furthermore, evaluating open-ended generation provides a more comprehensive measure of LLM performance than commonly used multiple-choice benchmarking, which can help in advancing the trust that can be placed within LLMs. Index Terms —Evaluation, fact extraction, faithfulness, hall- ucination, LLM, machine translation, question answering, RAG, summarization. I. I NTRODUCTION GENERATIVE AI has had signiﬁcant recent advancements and can be used to produce text, images or many different types of output [1]. Furthermore, it can serve as the engine in various intelligent applications, the most notable of which is Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs have become integral to numerous domains, leveraging their ability to understand and generate human language at a remarkable scale. These models, such as ChatGPT, BERT, and T5, have been applied across vari- ous ﬁelds, signiﬁcantly improving natural language understand- ing and generation [1]. Despite their impressive applications, LLMs are not always reliable, and they tend to hallucinate, i.e., occasionally produce responses that are clearly wrong or non-factual. These hallucinations necessitate the development of metrics and benchmarks that can assess the quality of LLM response to help detect and minimise hallucination. Through identiﬁcation of these hallucinations allows for their mitigation in a variety of manners, highlighting the importance of reli- able identiﬁcation. Applications Due to the broadness of tasks with which LLMs are often used for, there are several domains which have utilized unique strategies for assessing faithfulness, with these methodologies having been speciﬁcally chosen and optimised for the domain at hand. Faithfulness is a crucial evaluation criterion for all domains within the scope of this review, as users rely on the model to provide information that is factually correct and true to the original source otherwise problems will arise with varying levels of severity depending on the criticality of the task at hand. It can be challenging to deﬁne faithfulness universally due to the intricacies required across domains. For example, summa- rization requires the output to be aligned with the source mate- rial, which can be validated without the requirement of a ground truth. Whereas an open question answering (QA) task requires a ground truth to be provided for the faithfulness to be measured. The domains that are covered within this review are summa- rization, question answering and machine translation. In sum- marization, LLMs are used to condense large texts into concise summaries, offering practical applications in news aggregation, academic research, and legal documentation. Question answer- ing LLMs are used to retrieve and generate precise answers from vast datasets, powering search engines, customer service platforms, and knowledge systems Finally, machine transla- tion LLMs are used to produce semantically equivalent text in alternative languages, empowering the sharing of knowledge. Each of these applications, to varying levels of incurred burden, highlights the necessity of evaluating the faithfulness of the generated content, ensuring that outputs remain accurate and aligned with the source information. III. M ETRICS Faithfulness is often more difﬁcult to measure than other criteria like ﬂuency or grammatical correctness because it in- volves aligning both the factual content and the semantic mean- ing, where semantic meaning can be incredibly challenging to automatically evaluate. Ensuring faithfulness is critical for preventing misinformation, ensuring reliability in user-facing applications, and maintaining trust in AI-driven systems, espe- cially in knowledge-intensive or sensitive domains. This review focuses on evaluating automated metrics de- signed to assess the faithfulness of outputs generated by LLMs across a range of domains, including summarization, QA and machine translation. Each domain’s ubiquitous and automated metrics for assessing faithfulness, such as ROUGE [4], BLEU [5]and BERTScore [6], are discussed in addition to lesser-used metrics that may have only been used in speciﬁc domains and assessing their potential use case in alternative domains. Additionally, this review contrasts these automated metrics with human evaluation, which remains the gold standard for assessing faithfulness. Human evaluators can assess not only factual correctness but also nuanced meaning, context, and the intent behind model outputs. A. Overview of Evaluation Metrics Evaluation metrics for assessing the performance of language models can be broadly categorized into automatic and human evaluation. Automatic evaluation metrics, such as ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore, and fact-based approaches, are computational methods that quickly assess aspects like ﬂuency, faithfulness, or semantic similarity without human involvement. They are scalable and efﬁcient but may miss nuanced errors or factual inconsistencies. Human evaluation, on the other hand, involves human annotators judging the quality of generated outputs based on criteria like relevance, factual correctness, and coherence. While human evaluation is more reliable in capturing subjective and complex dimensions, it is resource-intensive, time-consuming, and prone to subjective variation. Human evaluation is very commonly used to validate the success of automatic metrics, whereby high Pearson correlation coefﬁcients show that an automatic metric makes similar judgements to a human evaluator. B. Faithfulness Metrics for Open-Ended Text Generation Open-ended text generation contrasts multiple-choice met- rics, through the requirement of unstructured text outputs. This makes the evaluation of faithfulness more challenging due to the ambiguity of what makes an output faithful. These metrics are more aligned with real-world scenarios, as it is commonplace for LLMs to be tasked with the production of open-ended text. 1) N-grams: N-gram metrics are commonly used in natu- ral language processing to evaluate the similarity between a generated text and a reference text by comparing overlapping sequences of words (n-grams). An n-gram refers to a contiguous sequence of “n” words or tokens. For example, a 1-gram (uni- gram) is a single word, a 2-gram (bigram) is a sequence of two words, and so on. N-gram metrics work by breaking down both the generated and reference texts into n-grams, then calculating the level of overlap. The higher the overlap, the more similar the texts are deemed. The ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evalu- ation) family of metrics is widely used for evaluating a wide va- riety of text generation tasks, likely due to its low computational requirements. However, these metrics do not consider synonyms or semantic understanding and can thus be too strict to reliably measure textual similarity. In addition to this, these approaches weigh all text equally (such as the use of connective words), even though a small number of n-grams convey the majority of semantic information [8]. Despite these well-known issues regarding n-gram metrics, such metrics remain popular among most domains of LLM faithfulness evaluation. 2) Exact Match (EM): Exact match (EM) as a metric is comparable to n-gram metrics, yet stricter, as it identiﬁes whether the reference text exactly matches the source/ground truth text. Thus, the output of this computation is binary, and offers no ﬂexibility, with several authors outlining such lim- itations [7],[12]. These factors make this metric very use- ful for some domains, such as multiple-choice QA, or entity- based QA where only short, concise, unambiguous answers are required. This rigidity of EM can be lessened to a degree through the implementation of a pool of valid answers, allowing for synonyms or aliases to still be deemed correct. However, this will incur additional burden on data collection. For more open-ended, ambiguous, or lengthier text generation tasks this metric is unlikely to be useful. For example, in the abstract summarization domain there will never be a single correct answer, and thus EM is unlikely to be able to evaluate an output as faithful, even if other metrics would deem it such [7]. However, when the desired output is simple, such as Yes/No responses, EM can often be the optimal approach due to the lack of ﬂexibility no longer being an issue [13]. 3) Lexical Match (LM): This metric is comparable to EM, but with less stringent requirements. Typically, only requiring the gold answer to appear within the output to be deemed as faithful. This approach mitigates some of the false negatives that can arise due to LLMs providing superﬂuous levels of detail when responding to a prompt. Lexical matching is only typically used within the QA do- main, due to the inherent binary nature of faithfulness within that area. As opposed to summarization, whereby there is greater ambiguity as to whether a summary conveys and entails the relevant information from a source. Several studies have utilized lexical matching as opposed to EM due to these beneﬁts, and state better suitability for QA tasks [7],[14]. 4) Question Generation: Within the domain of abstract sum- marization, question generation has been widely used as a measure of faithfulness [8],[15],[16],[17]. This methodol- ogy involves the generation of questions from both the model- generated summary and the corresponding source document, then the answers to these questions are compared to assess fac- tual consistency. If the answers to the questions generated from the summary align with those from the reference, the summary is considered faithful to the original text. This metric can output a score from 0-1, that shows the percentage of questions that had aligned answers (whereby a score of 1 demonstrates that every answer provided by the summary is in alignment with the answer provided by the source document) [8],[16]. Various authors have developed and implemented their own question-generation-answering-based metrics, such as FEQA, QAGS, Q2and QuestEval [8],[15],[16],[17]. However, they allsuffer from being dependent upon both the question-generation model, as well as the question answering model. As, if the generated questions are of low quality, such as through wording, ambiguity, or sparseness, then faithfulness is unlikely to be able to be evaluated reliably. Likewise, the performance is also de- pendent upon the question answering model, as questions can be incorrectly answered despite adequate context being provided, which can lead to unreliable faithfulness evaluation. These QA-based metrics are also focused on extractive in- formation, whereby questions can be answered directly through available text, making them less well-suited for tasks requiring more abstractive reasoning. Finally, these techniques also incur major computational overheads due to the additional models that are necessitated for both question-generation and question answering. 5) Embedding-Based: Embedding-based metrics are eval- uation methods that assess the similarity between generated text and reference text through comparing their semantic rep- resentations in a vector space. These metrics typically utilize pre-trained language models to generate embeddings for textual data, capturing deeper semantic relationships between the texts than can be captured with n-gram methodologies. Given both reference text and outputted text, an embedding- based evaluation would convert the tokens within both doc- uments into vectors, using a language model. The similarity between these embeddings can then be assessed using various computational measures. BERTScore is a commonplace metric, whereby the BERT language model generates the token em- beddings for both texts, then the cosine similarity is calculated between both sets of embeddings to provide a similarity score. However, other similarity calculations exist, such as the Mover- Score or Word Mover’s Distance (WMD) [18],[19]. These metrics measure similarity through calculating the minimum distance embedded words from one document would need to move to occupy the vector space inhabited by the embedded words from the opposing document. Furthermore, they show WMD to outperform BERTScore in the majority of tasks [18]. However, despite many authors stating superior performance from alternative embedding-based approaches, BERTScore is the most ubiquitous [18],[20]. Additionally, more modern token embedding models have been published, that can offer superior performance to BERT. Embedding-based methodologies have limitations, most no- tably regarding semantically similar tokens that do not convey the same fact. This can lead to issues when identifying faith- fulness as the embeddings for sentences may be highly similar to completely different sentences just because of similar subject matter [16]. 6) Fact Extraction: Fact extraction typically uses computa- tional means to identify facts from text and allows for faith- fulness to be assessed based on core factual elements rather than surface-level similarities, making it particularly effective in domains like question answering and summarization [21],[22]. Fact-tuples are a structured approach for evaluating the faith- fulness of generated text by extracting key facts from both the source and the output. These facts are typically represented as tu- ples (subject, predicate, object), capturing the essential relations and entities in the text. The methodology involves converting both the source and the generated output into sets of fact-tuples using information extraction techniques, then comparing them to measure the alignment between the source facts and the output. This comparison is commonly made using an F1 score, whereby the full list of fact-tuples available within both source and output determines the precision and recall [11]. However, this approach has the potential for incomplete or inaccurate tuple extraction, where complex or nuanced infor- mation might not be captured properly. This can be mitigated to some degree through deﬁned tuple output schema [11]. Fact- tuples also struggle with abstract or implicit knowledge, limiting their usefulness for more creative or generative tasks where direct fact alignment is less clear. Similarly to fact-tuple extraction is Named Entity Recognition (NER), which extracts key entities from source and generated text. Discrepant entities can be assumed to either be halluci- natory or missing, and thus not fully faithful. This evaluation technique has been used to calculate precision and recall of entities to assess faithfulness and demonstrated performance superior to that of n-gram approaches [23],[24]. 7) Graph-Based: The use of graphs to assess faithfulness can be achieved through the translation of textual data into graph-based data. This is commonly performed using Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR). AMR is a technique that con- verts sentences into structured graphs, where nodes represent concepts and edges represent relationships between those con- cepts. For faithfulness evaluation, this graph-based methodol- ogy involves constructing AMR graphs for both the source and generated text, then comparing these graphs to assess the alignment between the underlying meaning of the two texts. This graph-based approach captures deeper semantic struc- tures, allowing for an evaluation of whether the key concepts and relationships in the source are preserved in the generated output [25]. This approach allows for the assessment of both individual facts as well as the broader semantic and relational structure of the text, providing a more comprehensive view of faithful- ness. AMR-based evaluation can detect omissions, additions, or misrepresentations of important concepts. However, this technique can be complex and incur signiﬁcant computational costs when constructing and comparing graphs. Additionally, this methodology fails to evaluate faithfulness reliably when AMR is incorrectly parsed, which can occur for ambiguous or complex language. Additionally, small differences in graph structure may not always correspond to meaningful differences in faithfulness, leading to potential noise in the evaluation. 8) LLM Evaluators: For the purposes of this review, a metric is LLM-based if it utilizes a transformer-based architecture, with the exception of embedding-based techniques whereby whilstthey typically use a pre-trained LLM to assess similarity, it is distinct from a generation task. The methodologies differ based upon the domain in use, when language models are utilized as evaluators for faithfulness. The way in which LLMs typically operate as an evaluator is through an entailment approach. Entailment-based approaches to evaluate faithfulness utilize language models to determine whether generated text entails the source or reference text. These classiﬁcations are typically grouped into entailment, contradic- tion or neutral, though other studies have desired other outputs such as with a Likert 1-5 scale [26],[27]. If the generated text is deemed to entail the source, it is considered factually consistent and faithful. This method can capture high-level se- mantic relationships between the generated and reference texts, and it has been used in various forms as a faithfulness metric across multiple domains. LLMs have been used extensively as evaluators, commonly referred to as LLM-as-a-judge, and thoroughly trialed across various domains [28]. C. Human Evaluation Use of either Pearson or Spearman correlation to validate evaluation against human judgement is a common measure to validate new approaches, directly showing how well it aligns with human judgement which can be considered the gold stan- dard for evaluating faithfulness. [11],[16],[26],[29] D. Overview Each of the discussed metrics have various pros and cons, of- ten deﬁned by the data availability and the domain. These metrics are frequently used to evaluate the faithfulness of open-ended generated text. However, many of the most ubiquitous metrics are often favored for their scalability and speed but can fall short in capturing the nuances of faithfulness, especially when outputs involve abstract or complex reasoning. Even within singular domains, there is no clear, optimal metric, with various authors frequently ﬁnding different metrics to have the highest correlation with human judgement. Many datasets used are domain-speciﬁc and less relevant in other ﬁelds, as well as many metrics being utilized for speciﬁc domains. This arises a question as to the effectiveness of domain- agnostic metrics. Furthermore, due to the unique requirements each domain has, domain-agnostic datasets are unlikely to be feasible. IV . There are far more QA datasets that focus on short-form or multiple-choice based questions, requiring only a single entity as the answer, or a selection from a predeﬁned list. It is preferential for there to be multiple ground truth answers for a QA dataset, so that correct aliases can still be deemed as faithful. Multiple choice faithfulness is not within the scope of this review, which is focused on open-domain faithfulness, whereby natural text is generated to perform a task. Machine translation datasets that have been used to evaluate the faithfulness of translations can be Quality Estimation (QE) based or can use reference translations to assess. The former only requires the original text and the generated text in order to compute a score to represent the level of similarity, whilst the latter requires a high-quality translation through which similarity between this reference and the generated translation is calculated. Additionally, human annotations of faithfulness between parallel language text have been attained within this domain, though is less common than the others mentioned – likely due to the additional requirements for the annotators to be bilingual. However, several studies have still utilized correlation with human judgement to validate faithfulness metrics within this domain. B. Summarization Datasets As discussed, summarization datasets all contain a source document as well as a summary (either in the form of an overview of the source, or in individual claims or questions relating to the source). There are many datasets that have been trialed in this domain, each with unique merits and desirable properties. For example, the level of abstraction is a key element in summarization datasets, with the level of concision between the source and the summary being one of the main distinctions between datasets. In recent years, many summaries have been LLM gener- ated and received human evaluations as to their faithfulness to the source. These human evaluations can be extremely time- consuming to produce within this domain, due to the typically long length of source documents, yet they provide the best way to benchmark other metrics. There are few datasets that have high quality, human produced summaries, with a large portion of datasets containing summaries that are either not representative of the source (such as XSum [30], which uses the introductory sentence as the summary) or are LLM-generated summaries which can include inaccuracies [9],[27],[30]. Additionally, for the assessment of faithfulness in this domain, the provision of human-labelled faithfulness judgements is not commonplace, limiting the conﬁdence that can be placed within speciﬁc metrics and datasets. C. Question Answering Datasets Datasets within the question answering domain are character- ized by the presence of QA pairs, whereby a question is posed, with ground truth answer(s) provided. It is commonplace for several answers to be provided per question, due to the ubiquity with which questions have multiple correct answers, or entities have numerous valid aliases [7],[37],[38]. Datasets containing several answers per question can limit the rigidity with which both the exact match and lexical match methodologies operate, as well as for all additional metrics where the aliases may be closer to the outputted answer. Within the QA domain, the length of the required answer differs massively among the datasets, with the majority of QA datasets focusing on entity-based, short answers. This is likely due to the lessened ambiguity that is offered by entity-based QA, as well as the fact that commonplace metrics attain performance more comparable to humans when the answers are shorter, as metrics such as LM can attain stronger faithfulness results [7],[39]. The datasets present in Table II have been used to assess faithfulness, with no external context being required for the question to be responded to (i.e., reading comprehension, or dialogues).The majority of QA datasets that have been reviewed for this study are within the general knowledge domain, offering a wide variety of subject area. There are few datasets which contain long-form ground truth answers, with both TruthfulQA and WikiQA providing both correct and incorrect answers to a given question [39],[40]. Whereas the Natural Questions (NQ) dataset provides both short-form and long-form answers that have been provided by human annotators, all of which are deemed correct [38]. Mitigating Hallucination in LLMs Through the evaluation of faithfulness in LLM text gen- eration, many studies have used their evaluation protocols to mitigate the presence of hallucinations, and thus, increase the faithfulness of LLMs in their output. Some of these approaches are ubiquitous across domains, such as the use of external knowledge sources to ground the LLM in fact [58],[68], whilst others have shown promise in speciﬁc domains and not been trialed within others. External knowledge sources have been utilized heavily for the mitigation of hallucinations across several domains, such as question answering and knowledge-grounded dialogue eval- uation [58],[68],[69]. Alinejad uses a RAG-based approach, whereby LLMs are used to answer questions when provided with either gold context or retrieved context. These responses are then fed into an LLM evaluator to determine if they are aligned [58]. Thus, this approach can replace the need for gold answers in QA-based faithfulness evaluation, mitigating the major issue of ground truth quality, whilst also aiding in reliability. However, evaluation against human judgement would be necessary for further validation of this approach. Several studies have utilized prompting pipelines, allowing for the LLM to self-correct an unfaithful generation [70],[71]. This technique has been shown to improve the faithfulness of text generation in LLMs, and when operating in conjunction with accurate faithfulness evaluation could be used to mitigatehallucinations In addition to this prompting feedback approach, it has been well documented that the prompt supplied to an LLM has major inﬂuence on the quality of the generation, irrespective of whether a reﬁnement generation loop is used [72]. Future Directions There are several techniques that have been applied within the summarization domain to improve faithfulness evaluation that have not been trialed within long-form QA yet could provide similar beneﬁts. Data structuring and fact extraction techniques have been used to simplify summarized content and reduce the ambiguity [11],[21],[22]. To the best of our knowledge, these approaches have not been attempted in a QA domain. Through deﬁning a fact as a subject-relationship-object tuple, QA datasets can have ambiguity lessened, which would directly improve the exact match and lexical match approaches. This was shown by Goodrich within textual summarization and has been incorporated into QA datasets as performed by Mallen, yet no thorough analysis on this technique has been applied for QA [11],[37]. Some studies have shown LLM-based metrics to better cor- relate with human judgement than more traditional metrics within the assessment of multilingual translation [61],[62],[74]. However, LLM evaluators within this ﬁeld typically have skewed training data, due to the prevalence of English textual data, which can result in inconsistent evaluation capabilities across languages [62],[74]. Thus, a thorough evaluation assessing the limitations of these metrics for low resource languages would aid in the validation of these approaches. Due to the unique limitations that are apparent across all assessed metrics, the development of a fused metric that aims to mitigate the weaknesses prevalent across independent met- rics has the potential to correlate more strongly with human judgment across the various domains. This can be evidenced through the exact match and LLM evaluation metrics having contrasting limitations, high rates of false negatives and false positives respectively [7]. However, the fused metrics would likely need to be domain-speciﬁc due to the intricacies that each domain feature. Data structuring is a technique that has been demonstrated to improve the evaluation of faithfulness, primarily in the sum- marization domain, with the segmentation of text into extracted facts bolstering performance [11],[21],[22]. Similar techniques have been shown within dialogues, with several studies im- proving entailment accuracy and consistency upon the use of some level of fact extraction [73],[75]. Claim extraction-based faithfulness evaluation has been shown to be highly correlated with human judgement, surpassing other techniques used to improve these capabilities such as chain of thought prompting [51]. VII. C ONCLUSION In this review several domains are assessed for the respective approaches that have been taken to measure faithfulness, ﬁnding that there are many metrics unique to the intricacies posed within each domain. However, we ﬁnd that there is a lack of research performed in extending some of these metrics to new domains, where superior benchmarking capabilities could be achieved. This is most notable between summarization and question answering, whereby the data structuring approaches (which typically extract claims present in the source and have improved faithfulness evaluation) used within summarization studies could be migrated to question answering tasks. The do- mains that have assessed LLMs for their faithfulness evaluation capabilities have predominantly found that they are the metric that most closely aligns with human judgements. However, issues with LLM evaluators have been raised, most notably their tendency for false positives. In domains where lexical matching strategies are applicable a combinatorial metric could be utilized, mitigating the weaknesses of both LLMs and lexical matching for this task. Finally, many methodologies have been trialed to aid in mitigating the hallucinations that LLM generated text commonly suffers from, with the integration of an exter- nal knowledgebase (such as retrieval augmented generation) being both ubiquitous and successful in this task. Although other approaches exist which demonstrate an increase in the faithfulness of text generations, such as prompting frameworks which have also evidenced an increased faithfulness of outputs. It is through faithfulness evaluation that these techniques can be demonstrated to mitigate hallucinations, improving the suitabil- ity of LLMs for safety-critical scenarios, as well as to benchmark LLMs and validate their improvement for these use cases. Digital Object Identifier 10.1 109/ACCESS.2026.3668910 Domain-Adapted Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Technical Documentation: Enhancing Reliability and Faithfulness in Technical QA VERONIKA KRAINOVSKIKH AND TIMUR SAMIGULIN Department of Artificial Intelligence, ITMO University, 197101 Saint Petersburg, Russia Corresponding author: Veronika Krainovskikh (ronya.kraynova@gmail.com) This work was supported by the Ministry of Economic Development of the Russian Federation (IGK 000000C313925P4C0002) under Grant 139-15-2025-010. ABSTRACT This paper introduces a domain-adapted Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline specifically designed for technical question answering within industrial documentation. To overcome the limitations of generic retrieval systems in processing version-sensitive and semantically dense content, we develop a structured bilingual corpus of 20,000 manuals and fine-tune a dual-mode embedder (BGE- M3) with triplet loss and hard negatives. We further incorporate a two-stage reranking mechanism and an LLM-based query auditing module (LLM-Critic) to enhance retrieval precision and contextual adequacy. Experimental evaluation demonstrates substantial improvements in Recall@5 (from 0.67 to 0.86) and MRR (from 0.52 to 0.80), confirming the effectiveness of layered retrieval optimization in reducing ambiguity, strengthening grounding, and mitigating hallucinations. We have identified further tasks to address remaining challenges in managing multimodal content, resolving version disambiguation, and ensuring scalability for real-world deployment. INDEX TERMS LLM, RAG, question answering, technical, reliablitty, faithfulness, domain adaptation. I. INTRODUCTION Technical documentation, encompassing equipment man- uals, engineering standards [1], [2], [3], and regulatory guidelines [3], [4], [5], poses distinctive challenges for automated language processing. In contrast to general- domain text, technical documents undergo frequent revision, employ highly specialized terminology, and adhere to rigid structural formats with extensive cross-references and version dependencies. These characteristics constrain the effective- ness of traditional rule-based systems and ontology-driven pipelines, which, despite their precision, require substantial manual effort and lack adaptability. RELATED WORK Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a prominent approach for enhancing factual consistency in language models, particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks. Initially introduced by Lewis et al. (2020), RAG combined neural retrievers with sequence-to-sequence generators and demonstrated strong performance in open-domain QA using Wikipedia [6]. Subsequent research extended this paradigm to specialized domains, including biomedical and legal corpora to technical documentation — by incorporating domain-adaptive retrieval and fine-tuning strategies [20], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. Despite encouraging results, applying RAG to technical domains such as industrial manuals, engineering specifi- cations, and enterprise support documents entails unique challenges. These challenges include semantic ambiguity caused by overlapping terminology, redundancy arising from near-duplicate document versions, and evolving struc- tural formats that compromise retrieval performance. Initial attempts to address these limitations employed hybrid retriev- ers [26] and structured knowledge integration [27], [28], and demonstrated limited scalability and inconsistent robustness under frequent documentation updates [29]; however, these approaches frequently lacked unified latency reporting and sufficient in-domain baseline reproducibility, which reduces the transparency of comparative gains. Recent studies have identified retrieval optimization — not just better generation — as the critical bottleneck in domain-specific RAG systems. Empirical analyses in domains such as law, medicine, and aviation consistently attribute factual errors to irrelevant or misaligned retrieval [30], [31]. In response, several strategies have been proposed, including semantic chunking, dense-sparse retrieval ensembles, and two-stage reranking pipelines. These approaches are designed to improve top-k precision while maintaining acceptable latency, a property particularly critical in technical QA where traceability and factual grounding are essential.Although reranking and contrastive learning have improved retrieval precision, many methods remain depen- dent on large annotated datasets or handcrafted ontologies, limiting portability. Additionally, contrastive or end-to-end training approaches often suffer from overfitting to narrowly defined schemas. In parallel, hallucination mitigation strategies — such as context prepending and agent-based reranking — have demonstrated potential, yet remain difficult to evaluate consistently due to fragmented benchmarks and heterogeneous evaluation metrics. Taken together, these reviewed works underscore the central importance of retrieval precision for deploying RAG systems in technical domains. METHOD In technical QA tasks, users frequently require highly spe- cific, version-sensitive information from complex manuals, including configuration parameters, component tolerances, or troubleshooting procedures. DATA COLLECTION AND PREPARATION To support the proposed RAG pipeline, we constructed a corpus comprising over 20,000 industrial technical manuals from domains such as HV AC, automation, and electrical systems. The documents were preprocessed to preserve structural hierarchy (e.g., sectioning, tabular data), resulting in approximately 950,000 semantically coherent chunks for retrieval. A domain-specific QA dataset was then constructed using GPT-4o to generate realistic queries targeting configuration parameters, version-specific distinctions, and procedural instructions. Prompts explicitly required the model to include concrete component identifiers, model or firmware versions, numeric operating ranges, and to phrase questions in an operator-like style grounded in a single, retrievable pas- sage from the documentation. Redundant or semantically overlapping questions were removed using cosine similarity filtering, and the remaining samples were manually validated for domain relevance. Manual validation was performed by two domain experts through a consensus-driven review process. Each QA query was assessed using concrete inclusion criteria: (1) the answer must exist verbatim or be inferable without ambiguity within at least one document chunk retrieved from the indexed corpus, (2) the query must refer to a specific component, operational limit, or ordered procedure rather than a generic summary request, and (3) if numeric ranges, version identifiers, or cross- model distinctions are present in the source, the query andanswer should reflect them explicitly. We constructed the QA evaluation set by generating candidate operator-style questions from sampled manual passages and retaining only those answerable from a single retrievable chunk. text: V.International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET 2025) 3-6 July 2025, Paris-France Enhancing RAG Pipelines with Agent-Based Hallucination Detection and Guardrails Mechanisms Abstract— Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly more powerful and capable with time. By generating human-like text and understanding complex language patterns, they assist with tasks ranging from chatbots to content creation, revolutionizing how we interact with information. While they are very capable, they also face a significant challenge: hallucination. Hallucination refers to situations where LLMs generate factually inaccurate or misleading responses, veering off-the-rails from the truth. This research paper presents a comprehensive framework to address this issue, ensuring LLMs provide reliable and accurate information. The solution is twofold: implementing guardrails to keep LLMs on track and developing effective methods for hallucination detection. Two approaches are developed for the guard railing process and two more approaches are explored for the hallucination detection task. Each module will be explored in this research paper. By combining the above methods, the framework ensures that responses are factually correct and thoroughly vetted through hallucination detection checks. Making it unique, robust, and novel, increasing the reliability of LLM-powered applications. Keywords—Agents, Large Language Model (LLM), Hallucination, guardrails, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), Finetuning, Knowledge Graphs. I. INTRODUCTION In the day and age of such advancements in the Large Language Model’s (LLM) capabilities, multiple organizations and parties are interested in building custom chatbots to cater for their customers. The chatbot is required to follow a specific knowledge domain to respond to user queries. This introduces the need for Retrieval- Augmented Generation (RAG) that utilizes a retriever to fetch the required context based on the user query, which is followed by a generator module, which uses LLMs to generate a relevant response for the user query based on the retrieved context. In the RAG use case, which laid out the basis of this exploration was a RAG pipeline built for Apple 10K document for the fiscal year that ended on September 24, 2022. The document provides detailed financial information and performance analysis for investors and stakeholders.One of the key challenges in deploying LLMs for real-world RAG use cases is their tendency to hallucinate [1]. Hallucination in the context of LLMs usually refers to a situation where the model generates content that is not based on factual or accurate information [2]. The occasional generation of outputs that appear plausible but are factually incorrect significantly undermines the reliability of LLMs in real-world scenarios. Similarly, there have been instances where the LLMs give off- the-rail responses plaguing user trust in the generative AI- powered applications. For example, in a bank chatbot, the LLM might give responses questioning the user’s financial decisions, which is an unfortunate situation. To prevent from this occurring, guard rails are applied to the LLM, and it becomes of utmost importance for them to be adhered to. Various methods have been proposed to mitigate hallucination in RAG, including context injection and prompt engineering. RAGTruth [1] is a dataset specifically designed for hallucination detection which provides a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of hallucination detection methods. The development of high-quality datasets and advanced methods for hallucination detection is essential for ensuring the reliability and trustworthiness of LLMs in real- world applications. The approach mentioned in the paper addresses the limitations of LLMs, which often provide incorrect or outdated information due to their reliance on static training data. Particularly useful in scenarios where access to internal information enhances the accuracy and relevance of generated responses. More in-depth analysis can be found in this research paper. [8] The hallucination evaluation benchmark for large language models (HaluEval) is a large collection of generated and human- annotated hallucinated samples for evaluating the performance of LLMs in recognizing hallucinations.[5]. The construction pipeline of HaluEval involves a two-stage approach, sampling- then-filtering, to generate diverse hallucinated samples. The benchmark can facilitate research in understanding what types of content and to which extent LLMs tend to hallucinate, ultimately paving the way for building more effective and dependable LLMs in the future. Previous studies on hallucination detection have mainly concentrated on post-processing techniques for hallucination detection, which tend to be computationally intensive and limited in effectiveness due to their separation from the LLM's inference process. To overcome these limitations, MIND [9] is introduced, an unsupervised training framework that leverages the internal states of LLMs for real-time hallucination detection without requiring manual annotations. It processes the internal states of the LLMs using a simple MLP Layer for the classification task. HELM [9], a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs, featuring 6 LLM outputs and their corresponding internal states during their inference process. MIND outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in hallucination detection and gives a new perspective on LLM hallucination. Then the response triplets are compared with the user query + retrieved context and classified as “hallucinated” or “not hallucinated.” This methodology was updated for our solution with 4 major changes to optimize the results- •Replacing the LLMs with Agents powered by TLMs finetuned specifically for each of the steps. • Modifying the prompt completely for it to work with TLM Agents. Based on each of the judgements the classification of the whole response will be done. This was done to minimize the load on the TLM. Because Amazon made use of powerful LLMs like Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (GPT) 4 and Claude 3 Sonnet, they did not have to include this step. An in-depth explanation is available in the next section. •Lastly regex was applied to absolutely minimize the load on Agent, to classify the response as “hallucinated” or “not hallucinated” programmatically. Bigger models like GPT4 could easily handle the task of comparison and classification simultaneously, unlike the TLMs. Hence this step becomes necessary to extract the best performance out of TLMs in such a complex task. Document Store — where your knowledge lives You store all your domain documents (PDFs, text files, research papers) as chunked text pieces (e.g., 512-token chunks with 50-token overlap). Why chunking? LLMs can't read a whole 100-page PDF at once. You break it into small pieces so the retriever can find only the relevant piece. 2. Embedder — all-MiniLM-L6-v2 This converts text into vectors (lists of numbers) that capture meaning. Similar sentences get similar numbers. Why this model? 3. Chittagong, Bangladesh mahfuz csecuet@yahoo.com Abstract —For large language models (LLMs) to guarantee the trustworthiness and consistency of data, hallucination detection is essential. According to current research, the LLM model can generate false and inaccurate data that compromises the models’ dependability. A review on hallucination detection in LLMs was given in this paper. This study distinguished between internal and external methods for detecting hallucinations. While external models rely on external tools, internal approaches rely on signals within the model. In addition to outlining future research possibilities, this work describes methodological categories, frameworks, applications, and distinctions between various hallucination detection approaches. This article offers organized knowledge about reliable LLM model developments and hallucination detection. Index Terms —LLM, NLP, Reliability, Trustworthiness, Hallu- cination Detection, RAG, AI. I. I NTRODUCTION Large Language Models (LLMs) are currently tested in different text, image, and data processing applications, such as text summarization, sentiment analysis, virtual assistants, and content creation. Healthcare, banking, law, and education are just a few of the fields that use LLM models extensively [1], [2], [3], [4]. However, there were serious problems with LLM models, such as factual reliability or hallucinations, large computational costs, and problems with reasoning and ethics. When an LLM experiences hallucinations, it generates mate- rial that looks authoritative and well-written, but it contains false information, contradicting assertions, factual errors, or unreliable information. Current surveys don’t make a basic distinction between detection strategies that operate inside the LLM’s architecture and those that need outside documents and knowledge sources to be verified [5], [6], [7], [8]. Internal model-based and external knowledge-based techniques are the two primary categories into which this research has separated hallucination detection methodologies in order to address these problems. This study examined methods that examine model confidence scores, attention patterns, hidden state rep- resentations, uncertainty measurements, and consistency over several generations for internal model-based approaches. Thisarticle investigated fact-checking against knowledge bases, retrieval-augmented verification, cross-referencing with reli- able sources, and human-in-the-loop validation systems on the external knowledge-based side. Below is a list of this survey paper’s noteworthy contributions: •In order to automatically recognize hallucinations in writ- ings generated by LLM, this work presents a single tax- onomy that blends model-based and external knowledge- based approaches. •This survey study offers a thorough overview of au- tomated detection techniques in both categories, com- bining various approaches like fact-checking, retrieval- augmented verification, model confidence analysis, and hidden state representations. •This work highlights important issues and potential av- enues for future research while analyzing current stan- dards and datasets. text: [33]. V. K EYDIFFERENCES AMONG METHODS This study examined a large body of research on LLM methods for texts based hallucination identification. This study divided the current systems into two major groups: both ex- ternal knowledge-based detection systems and internal model- based detection systems. This paper demonstrated the differ- ences between them in terms of architectures, datasets, proce- dures, evaluation systems, and detection techniques. Internal model-based systems are computationally efficient for real- time deployment because they make use of the LLM’s internal operations without requiring external knowledge sources. The majority of internal systems rely on hidden state probing, attention pattern analysis, self-consistency analysis, and uncer- tainty estimates. The aforemntioned systems used transformer based architectures (GPT models, LLaMA) and different kind of probing classifiers. Different granularities can be provided by both token-level and sequence-level analysis. It can noted that hybrid approaches can combine several internal signals and also yield the best results. Retrieval systems and KBs must be intricately integrated in external knowledge-based systems to compare created content with reliable sources. The main types of this systems are benchmark evaluation platforms, fact- checking platforms, and RAG platforms. Retrieval systems and KBs are often incorporated with some architectures such as BERT, T5, and GPT versions. The evaluation approaches of internal and external systems differ significantly. AUROC, accuracy, precision-recall mea- sures, and correlation coefficients with human assessments are commonly used to assess internal model-based systems. Quantitative evaluation skills are demonstrated by performance indicators such as near 84 percent accuracy for hidden state probing and 0.89 AUROC for semantic entropy. External systems use a wider range of evaluation techniques, such as task-specific accuracy measures, factuality evaluations, and F1 scores. Benchmark analyses show significant differences in performance, with GPT-4 attaining near 82 percent detection rates and smaller models occasionally outperforming bigger ones in truthfulness tests. VI. L IMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK Hallucination detection still suffers from significant obsta- cles despite moderate advancements. Most methods are unable to generalize beyond certain domains. It can be noted that external verification techniques are still computationally costly. The current benchmarks are dispersed and lack consistent eval- uation. Biases are introduced by relying on outside resources. Internal uncertainty signals are frequently difficult for wider consumers to understand. Future research should focus on user-friendly interpretability, hybrid techniques incorporating internal and external clues. Further scopes for future research can include lightweight and accurate models, comprehensive benchmarks, spanning domains, and languages, and expanding detection to multimodal situations.VII. C ONCLUSION The reliable implementation of LLMs in safety-critical and knowledge-intensive applications is still fundamentally ham- pered by hallucination detection. In addition to highlighting representative techniques under each area, this survey article offered an organized taxonomy of detection methods that distinguished between internal and external approaches. Al- though current approaches show encouraging outcomes, there are still large gaps in scalability, trustworthiness, generaliza- tion, ethics checking, validation, and evaluation. Interdisci- plinary initiatives combining developments in NLP, knowledge representation, interpretability, and human-AI interaction are necessary to address these issues. Finally, developing reliable, accountable, and socially conscious AI systems requires effi- cient hallucination detection in addition to being a technical requirement.

text: Incorporating RAG for Factual Hallucination Detection Modeling in Intelligent Educational system Lei Zheng School of Computer Central China Normal University Wuhan, China 2248511201@qq.com Junmin Ye* School of Computer Central China Normal University Wuhan, China jmye@ccnu.edu.cn *Corresponding author Gang Zhao Hubei Key Laboratory of Digital Education Faculty of Artificial Intelligence In Education Central China Normal University Wuhan, China zhaogang@ccnu.edu.cnSheng Luo School of Computer Central China Normal University Wuhan, China luosheng@mails.ccnu.edu.cn Mengting Nan School of Computer Central China Normal University Wuhan, China 2238708584@qq.comYiliang Xie School of Computer Central China Normal University Wuhan, China tuanzzz0219@gmail.com Abstract—Factual hallucination isone of the key factors affecting learning effectiveness and knowledge construction in intelligent education system, and reducing factual hallucination can help develop learners' critical thinking and accurate knowledge acquisition. How to effectively detect factual hallucination in intelligent education system is a challenging issue in educational technology research. Based on this, this study proposed a factual hallucination detection model that incorporates knowledge retrieval enhancement and fine-tuning of large language model. First, an educational knowledge vector base is constructed from the collected knowledge datasets in the educational domain ; then , a factual illusion detection model is constructed by fusing the retrieval augmented generation(RAG ) technique and Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models(LoRA) fine-tuning method to optimize the large language model. We conducted experiments on a real dataset in the education domain, and the results show edthat this experimental model outperforms the existing models in terms of precision, recall , and F1 score for factual hallucination detection based on knowledge retrieval enhancement and model fine-tuning . Therefore, the experimental model in this paper is able to effectively detect factitious hallucination in intelligent education system, which lays the foundation for providing high-quality educational content. Keywords—intelligent educational system , factual hallucination, RAG I.INTRODUCTION Intelligent education system, as an important outcome of education information, are providing learners with intelligent and personalized education services by integrating advanced technologies [1] . These system play an important role in supporting distance learning and guaranteeing educational equity, showing great application value and development potential [2] . However, with the wide application of big language modeling in these system, the problem of factitious illusion of model output is becoming more and more prominent and has become a challenge that needs to be solved urgently. Factual hallucination refer to the possibility that the model may generate smoothly expressed but factually incorrect content, e.g., making up non-existent concepts, confusing historical facts, or giving false scientific explanations [3] . In educational scenarios, factual hallucination may lead to the dissemination of erroneous knowledge, reduce system credibility, and pose potential risks in certain specialized areas, thus seriously affecting learning outcomes and cognitive development [4] . Therefore, the establishment of an accurate and reliable detection mechanism for factitious hallucination has become a critical need to safeguard the quality of teaching and learning in intelligent education system 。. Based on this, this study proposed a new method for factitious hallucination detection in intelligent educational system. Both system have their own advantages, but both need to be further optimized to better serve educational scenarios. In recent years, generative model -based QA system have been widely used in intelligent education system b ecause they are closer to human interaction. These system are able to generate more natural and fluent answers and provide a personalized learning experience. However, most of the current generative language models are based on a large number of parameters to store knowledge, and there is a risk of over -generalization on untrained data, which is prone to generating some fictional "facts", thus triggering the phenomenon of "factual hallucination" and misleading the users[8]. B. Factual hallucination In the field of Large Language Models (LLMs), factual illusion refers to the generation of seemingly correct but factually incorrect content by the model, and this problem is manifested in tasks such as text summarization, Q&A, and dialog generation, which can have adverse effects such as misinformation for critical applications. For token -level detection , HADES constructs a dataset by perturbing Wikipedia text and proposes a baseline approach based on a pre -trained model [9] , while NPH trains factual critics and optimizes dialogue generation using an external knowledge graph to detect potentially illusor y entities [10] . For sentence -level detection, SelfCheckGPT [11] With the help of evaluating LLM self - consistency, which is detected by calculating consistency scores in multiple ways, ExHalder [12] Constructing frameworks and datasets for news headline h allucination, Harim+ [13] Reinterpretation of Decoder Target Definition Metrics Evaluating Summaries. HaluEval [14] proposes benchmarks and generates labeled samples to evaluate LLMs detection performance. These works provide ideas for solving the hallucin ation problem at different levels, but there are still challenges in detecting factual hallucination under the educational domain. The diversity and complexity of educational content and the high demand for accuracy make it difficult to directly apply trad itional hallucination detection methods. Therefore, the development of specific hallucination detection techniques for the educational domain, combining pedagogical theories and advanced natural language processing methods, has become an important directio n in the current research of intelligent educational system [15] . text: Title of the Project Design and Development of an Explainability-Driven Hallucination Detection Framework for OBline Retrieval-Augmented Generation We are not building a chatbot. We are building a knowledge system that retrieves documents, explains why they were selected, and only then generates answers. (No cloud APIs, No ChatGPT, No black-box answers) Problem Statement Large Language Models (LLMs) integrated with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks have significantly improved the factual grounding of generated responses by conditioning generation on retrieved documents. However, despite retrieval support, hallucinations i.e., generated statements that are unsupported or weakly supported by retrieved evidence remain a critical challenge, particularly in domain-specific and offline deployments. Most existing RAG systems primarily focus on improving retrieval quality or generation fluency, while hallucination detection is typically addressed using external fact-checking models, entailment classifiers, or post-hoc validation techniques. These approaches often introduce additional computational overhead, reduce interpretability, and are unsuitable for offline or resource-constrained environments. Moreover, hallucination detection mechanisms are commonly treated as independent modules, disconnected from the internal decision-making processes of the RAG pipeline. At the same time, recent advances in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) have enabled models to provide insight into retrieval relevance, attention patterns, similarity scores, and source attribution. However, these explainability signals are rarely exploited as primary features for hallucination detection and control, despite their direct relevance to assessing evidence support for generated content. This project addresses the following research problem: How can explainability signals generated within an offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework be systematically leveraged to detect, suppress, or control hallucinated outputs, while maintaining transparency, efficiency, and evidence grounding? The problem is characterized by several challenges: • Generated responses may include claims that are not fully supported by retrieved documents, even when retrieval quality is high. • Existing hallucination detection methods rely on heavyweight models or external services, limiting offline applicability. • RAG systems lack mechanisms to quantify and explain the degree of evidence support for individual generated statements.

text:
# BERTScore and Semantic Similarity Metrics

BERTScore is an automatic text-evaluation metric that measures how similar two pieces of text are in meaning, rather than in exact wording. It was originally proposed as a better alternative to older n-gram overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE, which count shared words or word sequences and therefore penalize a paraphrase even when it is perfectly correct. BERTScore instead encodes both texts (typically a "candidate" sentence and a "reference" sentence) into contextual token embeddings using a pretrained transformer such as BERT or a lighter model like DistilBERT, and then finds the best-matching pairs of tokens between the two texts using cosine similarity.

Concretely, for every token in the candidate text, BERTScore finds the reference token it is most similar to and records that similarity score; this produces a precision-like measure. It does the same in reverse — for every reference token, finding its best match in the candidate — producing a recall-like measure. The harmonic mean of these two directional scores gives BERTScore's F1, the number most commonly reported and used as a single similarity value between zero and one.

Because BERTScore operates on token-level embeddings rather than on whole-sentence embeddings, it captures finer-grained overlap than a single sentence-embedding cosine similarity would: a sentence can share most of its important content words with a reference while still being phrased differently, and BERTScore will reward that overlap where a cruder metric might not. This makes it a useful complementary signal alongside sentence-level cosine similarity and NLI entailment in a hallucination-detection pipeline — the three together check meaning-overlap at the sentence level (cosine), token level (BERTScore), and logical level (NLI entailment), so a claim that passes all three checks is supported in more than one independent sense, which is the rationale behind combining them into a single weighted "support score" rather than relying on any one signal alone.

One practical property of BERTScore worth noting is that it needs no training data of its own — it only needs a pretrained language model to produce embeddings — so it can be computed fully offline once that model is downloaded once, with no external API calls at inference time, which matches the offline design constraint of a local RAG hallucination-detection system.

text:
# Chunking Strategies for Document Retrieval

Before a document can be retrieved by a RAG system, it has to be broken into smaller pieces, or chunks, because embedding models have a maximum input length and, even below that limit, a very long passage produces a single embedding vector that blends together many unrelated ideas, making it a poor match for any specific query. Chunking is the step that decides how a raw document — a PDF, a Word file, plain text — gets split into the units that will actually be embedded, indexed, and retrieved.

The simplest approach, fixed-size chunking, splits text every N tokens (or words, or characters) regardless of sentence or paragraph boundaries. It is easy to implement and gives predictable chunk sizes, but it can cut a sentence or an idea in half at an arbitrary point, which may separate a claim from the context needed to understand or verify it. To reduce this problem, fixed-size chunking is almost always combined with overlap: instead of starting the next chunk exactly where the previous one ended, the next chunk begins some number of tokens before that boundary, so that content near a cut point appears in full in at least one chunk. A common configuration — 512 tokens per chunk with a 50-token overlap — balances chunk size against redundancy: large enough to preserve context within a chunk, with enough overlap that a boundary falling mid-sentence or mid-idea is still fully captured in a neighboring chunk, at a storage and indexing cost of roughly ten percent extra text.

More content-aware alternatives exist. Sentence- or paragraph-based chunking respects natural language boundaries, so a chunk never ends mid-sentence, at the cost of more variable chunk sizes. Semantic chunking goes further, using embedding similarity between adjacent sentences to decide where topic boundaries actually occur, splitting a document where the subject matter meaningfully shifts rather than at a fixed token count. Recursive or hierarchical chunking splits a document by structure first (sections, then paragraphs, then sentences) and only falls back to a fixed size if a structural unit is still too long.

Chunk size has a direct, measurable effect on retrieval quality. Chunks that are too large dilute the embedding with multiple topics, so a query about one specific fact inside a large chunk may not score highly enough against it to be retrieved, and even if retrieved, the surrounding irrelevant text adds noise to the context the generator receives. Chunks that are too small lose context — a sentence like "this reduces the error rate by half" is uninformative on its own without the preceding sentence identifying what "this" refers to. Choosing a chunking strategy and chunk size is therefore not a minor preprocessing detail but one of the first design decisions that shapes everything downstream in a retrieval-augmented pipeline, including how easy it later is to attribute a generated claim back to a single, coherent source passage.

text:
# Evaluation Metrics for Hallucination Detection Systems

Evaluating a hallucination-detection system means measuring how well it distinguishes supported claims from unsupported ones, using a labeled test set where the correct verdict for each claim is already known. The standard metrics for this kind of binary classification problem — precision, recall, F1, and AUROC — come from the broader machine learning literature but need some care in how they are applied here, because the two possible error types have very different real-world consequences.

Precision measures, out of everything the system flagged as hallucinated, what fraction actually was hallucinated. Recall (also called sensitivity) measures, out of everything that was actually hallucinated, what fraction the system caught. These two usually trade off against each other: a system can catch more hallucinations (higher recall) by flagging more aggressively, but that typically means also flagging some genuinely correct claims as hallucinated (lower precision), and vice versa. F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving a single number that only looks good when both are reasonably high, which is why it's commonly reported as the headline metric even though precision and recall individually tell a more complete story.

AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) evaluates a system across every possible decision threshold at once, rather than at the one threshold that was actually chosen. It plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the threshold sweeps from its most permissive to its most conservative setting, and the area under that curve summarizes how well the underlying support scores separate hallucinated claims from supported ones in general — a score of 1.0 means the two classes are perfectly separable by the score alone, while 0.5 means the score is no better than a random guess. AUROC is particularly useful during development, before a final threshold has been locked in, since it evaluates the quality of the scoring itself independently of any specific cutoff.

For a hallucination-detection system specifically, false negatives (a hallucinated claim that slips through as "supported") are generally considered more costly than false positives (a genuinely correct claim that gets unnecessarily flagged or blocked), because a missed hallucination can directly mislead a user who has no reason to distrust it, whereas an over-cautious block merely costs the user a moment of friction and a chance to consult the underlying evidence directly. This asymmetry is why many systems intentionally bias their threshold toward higher recall, accepting a larger number of occasionally-unnecessary flags in exchange for catching a larger share of actual hallucinations, and why reporting only accuracy (correct-verdict rate) without breaking it down by precision and recall can be misleading — a system could achieve seemingly high accuracy on an imbalanced test set simply by rarely flagging anything, while still missing most of the hallucinations that matter.
source_file: evaluation_metrics.md

text:
# Explainable AI (XAI) for Retrieval Systems

Explainable AI, or XAI, is the broad set of techniques for making a machine learning model's decisions understandable to a human, rather than leaving them as an opaque input-to-output mapping. In classical machine learning, XAI usually means explaining a single prediction — for example, which pixels of an image most influenced a classifier's decision, or which input features drove a model's output up or down. In retrieval and generation systems, the same underlying idea is repurposed to explain not a classification, but a retrieval decision and a generation decision: why was this particular document chunk retrieved for this query, and why did the model's answer take the shape it did.

Several explainability signals are naturally available inside a retrieval-augmented pipeline without requiring any extra specialized model. Similarity scores between the query and each retrieved chunk are themselves a form of explanation — they show, numerically, how confident the retrieval step was in each piece of evidence it surfaced. Chunk attribution — labeling exactly which source document and page a piece of retrieved text came from — turns a generated answer into something auditable: a user or reviewer can trace any claim back to its origin. Provenance scoring extends this idea to the whole answer, measuring what fraction of the generated response is actually traceable to retrieved evidence versus content that appears to have no clear source.

A more fine-grained technique is word-level saliency via leave-one-out perturbation: to estimate how much a specific word in a sentence contributes to that sentence's similarity to the retrieved evidence, the word is temporarily removed and the similarity is recomputed. If removing the word causes similarity to drop sharply, that word was carrying a lot of the sentence's evidential weight (it "anchors" the claim to the source); if removing it barely changes similarity, or even increases it, the word was not contributing evidential support and may be embellishment, filler, or an unsupported addition. Repeating this for every word in a sentence produces a saliency heatmap that visually distinguishes the evidence-grounded parts of a sentence from the parts that are not.

The significance of applying XAI this way to a hallucination-detection system is that it moves explainability from an optional add-on into the core detection mechanism itself. Rather than training a separate black-box classifier to predict "hallucinated or not" and then trying to explain that classifier's decision after the fact, the system's own retrieval and attribution signals — similarity, provenance, and saliency — are the features the hallucination decision is built on directly. This means every hallucination verdict the system produces already comes with a built-in, interpretable justification, rather than requiring a second explanation step bolted on afterward.

text:
# FAISS and Vector Databases

A vector database, or vector index, is a data structure purpose-built for storing large numbers of high-dimensional vectors and quickly finding the ones most similar to a given query vector. This is a different problem from a traditional relational database's exact-match lookups: with millions of 384- or 768-dimensional embeddings, comparing a query against every single vector one at a time (a "brute-force" or "flat" search) becomes slow, so specialized indexing structures and search algorithms are needed.

FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is an open-source library, developed by Meta AI, that implements a wide range of these similarity-search algorithms and is one of the most common choices for local, offline vector search because it runs entirely in-memory on a single machine with no external server or network call required. FAISS offers several index types with different speed/accuracy/memory trade-offs. The simplest, IndexFlatIP (inner product) or IndexFlatL2 (Euclidean distance), performs an exact brute-force search — guaranteed to find the true nearest neighbors, at the cost of scanning every stored vector, which is perfectly fine for corpora of a few thousand to a few hundred thousand chunks, but becomes a bottleneck at web scale. For much larger collections, FAISS provides approximate-nearest-neighbor structures such as IVF (inverted file index, which first clusters vectors and only searches the most promising clusters) and HNSW (a navigable small-world graph), which trade a small amount of accuracy for large speed gains.

When embeddings are L2-normalized (rescaled to unit length) before being added to the index, an inner-product search is mathematically identical to a cosine-similarity search, which is why many RAG pipelines pair IndexFlatIP with normalized Sentence-BERT embeddings to get a fast, exact cosine-similarity retriever without any extra math at query time.

Because FAISS keeps everything in memory and needs no server process, database credentials, or internet connection, it is well suited to offline and privacy-sensitive RAG deployments: the entire retrieval stack — embedder plus index — can be packaged and run on a single laptop. The trade-off is that a FAISS index alone does not automatically stay in sync with new or deleted documents; an application has to explicitly re-embed and re-add (or rebuild) the index whenever the underlying document store changes, which is exactly why a RAG system's "build index" or "re-index" step is typically a separate, explicit action rather than something that happens automatically in the background.
