text:
# Hallucination in Large Language Models

In the context of large language models, hallucination refers to generated content that is fluent and confident-sounding but factually incorrect, unsupported by any source, or internally inconsistent with the prompt. The term is borrowed loosely from psychology, but in machine learning it describes a specific failure mode: the model is not malfunctioning in any obvious way, and the output usually reads as perfectly natural language — the problem is purely that the claims it contains are not true or not grounded in real evidence.

Researchers generally split hallucinations into two broad categories. Intrinsic hallucinations directly contradict the source material the model was given (for example, a summary that states the opposite of what the source document says). Extrinsic hallucinations introduce information that cannot be verified from the source at all — not necessarily false, but simply invented or added from the model's general training knowledge rather than the provided context. In a retrieval-augmented system, extrinsic hallucination is the more common and more dangerous failure, since a model may blend real retrieved facts with plausible-sounding but unretrieved details, making the fabricated parts hard to spot without checking each claim against the actual evidence.

The causes of hallucination are still an active research area, but several contributing factors are well documented. Language models are trained to predict plausible next tokens, not to verify truth, so a fluent continuation is optimized for over a correct one whenever the two diverge. Training data itself contains errors, contradictions, and outdated information, which models can absorb as if it were established fact. Long or ambiguous prompts increase the chance that a model loses track of exactly what it was given versus what it "remembers," and models are also known to exhibit sycophancy — generating an answer that matches what the question seems to expect, even if that answer is not well supported.

Mitigation strategies broadly fall into two groups. The first works before or during generation: grounding the model in retrieved evidence (retrieval-augmented generation), using more constrained decoding, or prompting the model explicitly to say "I don't know" when it lacks support. The second works after generation: verifying each generated claim against evidence using entailment classifiers, semantic similarity scores, or a second "fact-checking" model pass, and then deciding whether to show, flag, or block the output based on that verification. A hallucination-detection framework that blocks or partially suppresses a response when verification fails — rather than only flagging it after the fact — sits in this second category, and is generally considered a stronger safeguard for high-stakes or offline deployments where a human reviewer may not be available to catch every unflagged error.
source_file: hallucination_in_llms.md

text:
# Large Language Models and Local Inference with Ollama

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, almost always based on the transformer architecture, trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token in a sequence. At sufficient scale, this simple training objective gives rise to broad capabilities: answering questions, summarizing, translating, and following instructions, even though the model was never explicitly trained to do any one of those tasks directly. Well-known LLM families include the proprietary GPT models accessed through an API, and open-weight models such as Meta's LLaMA family and Mistral AI's Mistral models, whose weights can be downloaded and run on a user's own hardware rather than only through a cloud provider.

Running an LLM "locally" means the model's weights are loaded and the forward pass is computed on the user's own machine rather than sent to a remote server. Ollama is a tool that makes this practical for non-specialist users: it packages open-weight models (Mistral, LLaMA 3, Phi-3, and many others) into a single downloadable artifact, handles quantization (compressing the model's numeric weights to use less memory, typically with only a small accuracy cost), and exposes a simple local HTTP API — by default at http://localhost:11434 — so that any application can send a prompt and receive a generated completion with a single request, without the application needing to know anything about how the model itself is loaded or run.

Local inference has direct consequences for how a retrieval-augmented system can be deployed. Because no data leaves the machine, it is suitable for privacy-sensitive or regulated environments where sending documents to a third-party API would be unacceptable. There is no per-token or per-request cost, no rate limit imposed by an external provider, and no dependency on network connectivity, which matters for genuinely offline deployments. The trade-off is hardware: open-weight models run through Ollama are typically smaller than the largest proprietary models, and inference speed depends entirely on the local machine's CPU or GPU, so a response that takes a fraction of a second from a well-provisioned cloud API might take tens of seconds on a laptop, especially the first time a model is loaded into memory.

For a hallucination-controlled RAG system, the choice of local generator interacts directly with the detection layer: the LLM generator is explicitly instructed, via its system prompt, to answer only from the retrieved context and to say so explicitly when the context is insufficient — but this instruction is a request, not a guarantee, which is exactly why a separate, independent verification step (checking the generated answer against the evidence after the fact, rather than only trusting the prompt) remains necessary even when the generator has been told to behave conservatively.

text:
# Natural Language Inference (NLI)

Natural Language Inference is the task of determining the logical relationship between two pieces of text: a premise and a hypothesis. Given a premise, a model classifies the hypothesis into one of three categories — entailment, meaning the premise logically supports or implies the hypothesis; contradiction, meaning the premise and hypothesis cannot both be true; or neutral, meaning the premise neither supports nor contradicts the hypothesis. NLI began as a standalone benchmark task in NLP research, with datasets such as SNLI and MultiNLI, but the same entailment classifiers have since become a core building block of hallucination detection.

The connection is direct: if a generated sentence is treated as the hypothesis and a retrieved evidence chunk is treated as the premise, then checking whether the evidence entails the generated sentence is exactly the question a hallucination detector needs answered. A high entailment score means the retrieved document genuinely supports the claim; a contradiction score means the generated sentence conflicts with the evidence (a particularly serious failure, since the model has effectively invented the opposite of what its own sources say); and a neutral or low-entailment score means the sentence is going beyond — or drifting away from — what the evidence actually states, the hallmark of an unsupported or fabricated claim.

Cross-encoder NLI models, such as the DeBERTa-based cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small model, process the premise and hypothesis together in a single forward pass through the transformer, which lets the model's attention layers directly compare words and phrases across the two texts. This gives cross-encoders noticeably higher accuracy than comparing separately computed sentence embeddings for this task, at the cost of being slower, since every premise-hypothesis pair must be run through the model together rather than reusing pre-computed vectors. For hallucination detection, where each generated sentence is checked against only a handful of retrieved chunks rather than an entire corpus, this extra cost per comparison is manageable, which is why cross-encoder NLI models are a practical and popular choice for this specific verification step even in otherwise latency-conscious pipelines.

A practical design decision in NLI-based hallucination detection is which of the three output probabilities to use as the "support" signal. Most systems take the entailment probability directly, sometimes subtracting the contradiction probability, so that a sentence that is actively contradicted by evidence scores even lower than one that is merely unaddressed by it — a distinction that matters because contradicted claims are typically the most damaging kind of hallucination to let through unflagged.

text:
# Prompt Engineering and Grounded Generation

Prompt engineering is the practice of carefully designing the instructions and context given to a language model in order to steer its output toward a desired form, tone, or level of factual caution, without changing the model's underlying weights. Because a language model's behavior is shaped entirely by the text it is conditioned on, the exact wording, ordering, and structure of a prompt can materially change whether its response is accurate, well-formatted, or appropriately cautious.

In a retrieval-augmented system, prompt engineering plays a specific, load-bearing role: the prompt is what tells the model to answer using only the retrieved context rather than its own general training knowledge, and what tells it how to behave when that context is insufficient. A typical grounded-generation system prompt states the rule directly — answer only using the provided context, and if the context does not contain enough information, say so explicitly rather than guessing — and this single instruction is one of the main levers available for reducing hallucination before generation even happens, as opposed to catching it afterward with a separate verification step.

Several concrete techniques recur across grounded-generation prompts. Explicitly labeling the retrieved passages within the prompt (for example, tagging each one with its source filename and page number) makes it easier for the model to cite sources correctly in its answer, since the citation information is right there in its input rather than something it has to recall. Keeping the instruction to "say I don't know if unsure" close to the start of the prompt, and repeating it near the question itself, tends to make the model more likely to actually follow it, since instructions closer to the point of generation have more influence than ones buried far earlier in a long prompt. Lowering the generation temperature — the parameter controlling how much randomness is injected into token selection — also reduces the model's tendency to embellish or wander from the given context, at some cost to the variety and naturalness of its phrasing.

It is important to be clear about what prompt engineering can and cannot guarantee. Instructing a model to stay grounded in context changes the probability that it behaves conservatively, but a language model has no mechanism that enforces an instruction the way a rule in traditional software would — it can still ignore the instruction under certain inputs, blend retrieved facts with unretrieved ones, or misjudge whether the context is actually sufficient. This is why, in a rigorous hallucination-detection pipeline, prompt engineering is treated as a first line of defense that reduces the frequency of unsupported claims, while an independent, model-external verification step — checking the generated text against the evidence after generation — remains the mechanism that actually catches whatever the prompt failed to prevent.

text:
# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, is an architecture for building language-model systems that combines two separate capabilities: a retriever that searches an external knowledge source, and a generator that produces natural-language text. Instead of relying only on facts memorized during training, a RAG system looks up relevant passages from a document collection at query time and feeds them to the language model as context before it writes an answer.

The typical RAG pipeline has three stages. First, documents are split into smaller chunks and converted into vector embeddings using an embedding model, then stored in a vector index. Second, when a user asks a question, the same embedding model converts the query into a vector, and the index returns the most similar chunks by a distance or similarity measure such as cosine similarity. Third, the retrieved chunks are inserted into a prompt along with the original question, and a large language model generates an answer conditioned on that retrieved evidence.

The main motivation for RAG is grounding: a language model trained purely on its pretraining data can produce fluent but factually incorrect statements, a failure mode generally called hallucination. By forcing the model to base its answer on retrieved, verifiable text, RAG reduces (though does not eliminate) this risk, and it also makes answers auditable, since the system can cite exactly which document a claim came from. RAG additionally allows a system to stay current and domain-specific without retraining the underlying model — updating the knowledge base is as simple as re-indexing new documents.

RAG systems can run entirely offline when every component — the embedding model, the vector index, and the generator — is hosted locally rather than through a cloud API. This is attractive for privacy-sensitive or air-gapped deployments, such as legal, medical, or defense settings, where documents cannot leave the organization's own infrastructure. Running offline typically means smaller, quantized open-weight models (served through a runtime such as Ollama) rather than very large proprietary models, trading some generation fluency for data privacy and zero marginal API cost.

RAG is not a guarantee against hallucination by itself. A language model can still ignore the retrieved context, misread it, or generate a claim not actually supported by any retrieved chunk — sometimes called "RAG hallucination" to distinguish it from hallucination caused purely by a model's own parametric knowledge. This is precisely the gap that hallucination-detection layers, such as entailment classifiers or similarity-based verification, are designed to catch: they check, after generation, whether each sentence in the answer is actually backed by the evidence that was retrieved for it, rather than simply trusting that retrieval plus generation together produced a faithful response.

text:
# Sentence Embeddings and Semantic Search

A sentence embedding is a fixed-length numeric vector that represents the meaning of a piece of text, produced by a neural network trained so that texts with similar meaning end up close together in the resulting vector space, while unrelated texts end up far apart. Unlike older bag-of-words representations, which only capture which words appear, embeddings capture semantic similarity — two sentences phrased completely differently but meaning the same thing will still have vectors that point in nearly the same direction.

The Sentence-BERT family of models, including all-MiniLM-L6-v2, is one of the most widely used approaches for producing these embeddings efficiently. It fine-tunes a transformer encoder (a distilled, smaller version of BERT-style architectures) using a contrastive or similarity-based training objective, so that encoding a sentence takes a single forward pass rather than the pairwise comparisons earlier BERT-based similarity methods required. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 specifically produces 384-dimensional vectors, is only about 80 megabytes, and runs comfortably on a CPU, which makes it a practical default for offline or resource-constrained retrieval systems rather than requiring a GPU or a cloud embedding API.

Once documents and queries are both converted into this shared vector space, semantic search becomes a nearest-neighbor problem: given a query vector, find the document vectors closest to it. Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity, which looks only at the angle between two vectors and ignores their magnitude, or with the dot product when vectors are first normalized to unit length (in which case the two measures become equivalent). This is why retrieval pipelines typically normalize embeddings before indexing — it lets a fast dot-product search stand in for cosine similarity without extra computation at query time.

Semantic search improves substantially on older keyword-matching search because it can retrieve a relevant passage even when the query and the passage share almost no exact words — for example, a query about "how to reduce fabricated answers" can retrieve a passage about "hallucination mitigation techniques" even without a single overlapping keyword, because the two phrases are embedded close together. This property is what makes sentence embeddings the standard first stage of a modern retrieval-augmented generation pipeline: they decide which chunks of a document collection are even considered before the language model sees anything.

text:
# Tri-State Decision Control for Generated Answers

A decision controller is the component of a hallucination-aware pipeline that takes the per-sentence support scores produced by the detection layer and turns them into a final action: show the answer, show it with caveats, or withhold it. Rather than a simple binary pass/fail, many systems use a tri-state scheme with two thresholds, producing three possible outcomes for each generated sentence or for the response as a whole.

In a typical tri-state scheme, a support score at or above a high threshold (for example 0.75) is classified as fully Supported, meaning the evidence strongly backs the claim, and the sentence is shown along with its citation. A score between a medium threshold (for example 0.50) and the high threshold is classified as Weakly Supported: the evidence partially backs the claim, or backs a related but not identical claim, so the sentence is still shown but flagged with a warning so the reader knows to treat it with more caution. A score below the medium threshold is classified as Hallucinated: the evidence does not meaningfully support the claim, and the sentence is either removed from the shown answer or the entire response is withheld, depending on how severe the failure is.

The decision to block an entire response, rather than just removing the unsupported sentence and showing the rest, typically depends on a ratio: if more than some fraction of a response's sentences (a common choice is fifty percent) are classified as Hallucinated, the system concludes that the response as a whole is unreliable — even the "supported" sentences that remain may have been generated in a context where the model was already drifting from the evidence — and suppresses the entire answer rather than presenting a partial one that could still mislead. This is a deliberately conservative design choice: a system that always shows whatever fraction of an answer happens to check out can still cause harm if the surviving fragments, taken together, paint a misleading picture, whereas a system that withholds a low-confidence answer entirely and instead surfaces the raw retrieved evidence lets the user judge the source material directly.

The two thresholds themselves are tunable parameters, not fixed constants, and the right values depend on the application's tolerance for false blocks versus false passes. Raising the high threshold makes the system more conservative — fewer answers qualify as fully supported, reducing the chance that a subtly unsupported claim slips through as "Supported," at the cost of flagging more genuinely correct answers as only weakly supported. Lowering the medium threshold has the opposite effect: fewer answers get blocked outright, at the cost of letting weaker evidence still result in a shown (if flagged) answer. Because this trade-off has no universally correct setting, a well-built system exposes both thresholds as adjustable parameters rather than hard-coding them, so the same detection scores can be re-classified under a stricter or looser policy without re-running any of the underlying models.
